story:
Amelia found a book about turtles at the library. She loved the turtles very much. She did not want to give the book back. She wanted to keep it forever.

"Look, Mother," she said. She opened the book. "The words tell about the turtles." She turned the first page. Then the next page. Then the next. "You read this way, front to back," she said. She pointed at a word. "That word says shell. I can see it."

Mother smiled. "You can take the book home," she said. "But we must bring it back. Other kids want to read it too."

Amelia held the book tight. "But it is my turtle book," she said.

At home, Amelia read the turtle book seven times. Then she read it two more times. On the last day, Mother said, "Time to take the turtle book back."

Amelia waved to the book. "Bye bye, turtle book," she said. She put it in the bag. At the library, she put it on the shelf. A boy picked it up right away.

"He can read it now," said Amelia. "Because I brought it back. That is why."

Then she ran to find a book about frogs.

Scarlett wanted to help make soup. She stood by the stove with Mama. The pot sat on the hot burner. Mama said, "We look with our eyes. We do not touch the pot." Scarlett looked at the steam. It went up, up, up.

Mama turned off the stove. "Now we wait," she said. Scarlett waited. She watched the steam go away, little by little. It took a long time. Scarlett waited some more. Then Mama touched the pot. "It is warm now," she said. "You can touch the side."

Scarlett put one finger on the pot. It was warm, not hot. "The burner was hot," said Scarlett. "Now the pot is not hot. The steam went away because the stove is off." Mama smiled and gave the soup a stir. An onion seed rolled round and round in the pot. After lunch, Scarlett was tired. She climbed onto her bed. "I helped," she said, and closed her eyes.

Aubrey sat down for dinner. "Soup night!" said Mama. Aubrey sniffed with her nose. She could smell carrots. Her ears heard slurps. Her eyes saw steam rise. But there was a problem. Aubrey's nose was stuffy today. She took a taste with her tongue. The soup had no taste at all.

She held her nose shut with her fingers. She tasted again. Still nothing. Then she let her nose go and sniffed a big sniff. Ah! Now the carrot taste came in! "Mama, my tongue needs my nose!" said Aubrey. "What a lucky nose," said Mama.

Daddy passed her bread. Aubrey touched it with her hands. Warm and soft. She counted on her fingers: "Eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands. Eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands." Then she took one more slurp. "Yummy," she said. "The nose did it."

Livia went to the art gallery with Papa. She saw a big red circle on the wall. "Red," said Livia. Then she saw a blue square. "Blue!" Then a yellow sun. "Yellow!"

Livia wanted to paint too. A kind lady gave her a small brush. Livia painted with red. Then she painted with blue. "Oh no," said Livia. "Now it looks dark. Kind of yucky!"

But then she looked again. The red and blue touched. Where they touched, it turned purple! Livia pointed. "Red and blue make purple!" Papa smiled. "It made a new colour," said Livia.

A boy dropped his brush. It made a loud noise. Livia picked it up and gave it back. "Here you go," she said. The boy smiled. Livia painted one more purple dot, big and round.

Thomas wanted to wash his hands. He climbed to the sink in the bathroom. Mama stood close by him.

Thomas turned the tap. Steam came up. He pulled his hand back fast.

"Too hot!" said Thomas.

Mama turned the other tap. Cold water ran out. She put his hand under it. The water felt cool and nice now.

Thomas rubbed the rough towel on his wet hands. Then he saw Mama's cookie on the shelf. He wanted it, but he did not touch.

"Please, Mama?" said Thomas.

Mama gave him a bite. It was sweet.

"I forgot the cold tap," said Thomas. "Hot water comes first. Cold water makes it okay."

Mama smiled. "You can call me next time."

Thomas took her hand. "Together," he said.

Nora wanted to go outside. She wanted to pretend she was a sheep on the big green hill. But first she needed her coat.

Mom said, "You can try it yourself." Nora pushed her arm in one sleeve. She pushed her arm in the other sleeve. One, two arms! Now the zipper. She pulled it up. The zipper did not move. It was stuck at the bottom.

Nora looked closely. The two sides were not in the little slot. She pushed the point down into the slot. Click! She pulled the slider up. Zip, zip, zip, all the way to her chin!

"The zipper needs the slot," said Nora. "That is why it was stuck." Mom smiled.

Outside, the wind was loud. Nora ran and pretended to be a sheep. "Baa!" she said. Her coat stayed warm and zipped tight.

Miles went to the library with his dad. They rode the big bus. The bus was heavy and slow. At the library, Miles saw a tablet on a small table.

He wanted to draw a cat on it. He tapped the screen once. Nothing happened. He tapped again. Still nothing. Then he held the little round button for a long count. The screen woke up. "Oh, it needs a long hold," said Miles.

He found the drawing app. It had a yellow spot. He touched the yellow spot. Now he could draw. He drew a cat with one ear and a happy tail. Then it was time to go. Miles pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He put the tablet back on the shelf. His coat would hang on the hook by the door. "Why did the screen sleep?" he asked. "Because I held the button," said Miles. He waved to the tablet. "Bye, bye, tablet."

Cooper wanted the red truck. His sister Mia had the red truck. She pushed it on the rug. Cooper grabbed the truck. Mia said, "My turn!"

Cooper held the truck tight. Mia began to cry. She sat down and looked away. Now Cooper had the truck, but no one to play with. The rug was quiet. That was not fun.

Cooper looked out the window. Rain made the street wet. A car went by. Its wheels did not slip. The rain slid off the wet road. Cooper watched it for a long time.

Then he had an idea. He pushed the truck to Mia. "Your turn," he said. Mia smiled. She pushed the truck back. "Your turn," she said. The truck went back and forth, back and forth.

"Now we both play," said Cooper. "Because we take turns."

Sara went to the library with Dad. She saw a big shelf of books. She wanted the bear book on the top shelf. It was too high. Dad said, "I will get it for you." Sara felt excited. She jumped up and down.

Then a boy ran by. He knocked the bear book down. The book fell on Sara's foot. Sara felt angry. Her face got hot and mad. She wanted to yell. But then she saw the boy's face. His mouth turned down. His eyes were wet. He felt sad. He did not mean to knock the book.

Sara looked at his sad face. She held out her hand. "Come look at bears with me," she said. The boy smiled big. Sara could tell he felt happy now. They sat down together. Sara opened the book. "Look!" she said. "Wild bears live in the woods." Then Dad said, "Snack time at the store." Sara and the boy ran to the door.

Declan ran to the window at daycare. He wanted to play in the puddles. But the puddles were gone. "Where did the water go?" he asked. He looked and looked. The sun was warm on his hands. "The sun dried it up," he said. Yesterday it had rained. Yesterday the puddles were big. Today was different. Today the sun was out, and the ground was dry.

Declan had a problem. He wanted to splash, but there was no puddle now. Miss Amy smiled. "You can splash later," she said. "We will water the flowers soon." Declan waited. Then it was time. He held the little watering can. Water spilled onto the stones. A small puddle grew. Declan stamped his boots. Tap, tap, tap! His sock began to stick to his wet shoe. He laughed. "Tomorrow I can do it again," he said. "Tomorrow comes after I sleep." Then he tipped the can one more time.

Charlie stood on her step stool in the kitchen. She wanted to make her own breakfast. "Can I do the butter, Mama?" she asked. "Yes, let's try," said Mama.

Charlie looked at the toast. It had a flower on the plate next to it. She pushed the hard butter with her knife. The toast tore. "Oh no," said Charlie. "Why did it rip?" Mama put the butter dish near the warm toaster for a minute. Then Charlie tried again. The butter was soft now. She made one thin line. Then two thin lines. Then three. "Soft butter does not rip it," said Charlie. "It ripped because the butter was cold."

Next came the milk. Charlie held the little jug with both hands. She tipped it fast and milk spilled out. One drop, two drops, a little puddle. "Too fast," said Charlie. She tried again, slowly. Tip, tip, tippy tip. The milk went into the cup and nothing fell. "Slow pouring keeps it in," she said.

Charlie sat down and took a big bite of toast. She looked at her cup, full to the top. "I made breakfast all by myself," she said. Then she drank her milk.

Madeline sat in a big chair at Grandma's house. Today she was three. On the cake were three little candles. The flames were tall and orange.

"Blow out your candles," said Grandma. Madeline blew a little puff. One candle went out. Two flames were still dancing. Grandma fanned the smoke away with her hand.

Madeline puffed her cheeks. She took a very big breath, all the way down to her tummy. Then she blew hard. Fwoosh. The last two candles went out. "The big breath did it!" said Madeline. Everyone clapped. Grandma cut the cake. The first big piece was for Madeline.

The cake was cool from the fridge, and sweet on her tongue. Her cousin Ben dropped his fork. Madeline picked it up and gave it back to him. "Thank you, Madeline," said Ben. Then everyone sang the birthday song one more time, just for fun. Madeline sat up tall in her chair and sang too, as loud as she could.

Maria put on her new hat. She ran to the backyard with Dad. "Stay close," said Dad. "Stay close," said Maria.

Maria saw the grill. It was hot. Daddy had cooked on it. Maria held out her hand. She felt the heat. She pulled her hand back fast. "Hot!" she said. "I will not touch." Dad said, "Good girl. Hot things can hurt you."

Then Maria saw a puddle. She put her hand in it. "Cold," she said. She laughed. She wiped her wet hand on her towel. Maria looked at the grill again. "The grill is hot because Daddy cooked on it," she said. "The puddle is cold because it is water." Dad picked her up. "Let's stay close and find more cold things." Maria held Dad's hand tight.

Alice went to the store with her mom. Her little brother was hungry. He wanted apples for snack time.

Mom said, "Pick six apples, please." Alice knew the counting song. She sang it every day. She put apples in the bag. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. Then she put one more. "Six!" The bag was full.

At home, her brother ate an apple. He smiled a big smile. Alice gave one to Mom too. Then she counted what was left. "One, two, three, four." Four apples in the bowl. "Four, because we ate two!" she said. Mom clapped her hands. "You counted so well." Alice tried a little bow. Her brother giggled and held up his apple core.

Lydia went to the big game with Mama, Papa, and Gran. The stadium was so big. Lydia held Gran's hand. They found their seats. One, two, three, four seats in a row.

The crowd began to stand up. Then they sat down. Then the next people stood up. It was a wave, and the wave went all the way around. "One, two, three, up!" said Papa. Lydia stood up too. The wave came to her. She jumped up, then sat down. Her tummy felt jumpy and happy. The wave came again. "One, two, three, up!" This time Lydia was last in her row. She popped up, and the wave kept going.

After the game, Lydia skipped to the gate. "The wave moves because we all stand up," she said. "One, two, three, up!" said Gran, and she stood up right there. Lydia laughed and stood up too.

Emilia went to the store with Dad. She saw a big bin of apples. She wanted a red apple for Grandma's present. A boy was there first. He picked up an apple slowly.

"Wait for your turn," said Dad. Emilia stood still. The boy took one apple. Then he looked at Emilia. He held out a big red apple. "You can have this one," he said.

Emilia took the apple with both hands. "Thank you," she said. She put the apple in the cart. The cart wheels went deep in the rug by the door. Dad laughed. At home, Grandma bit the apple. "So sweet," said Grandma. "He shared, so I got my turn," said Emilia. Dad smiled and hugged her.

Chloe sat at the kitchen table. Dad had put out five little cups. "Let's play the sense game," said Dad. "Guess what each cup is. Then tell me which body part you used."

Chloe picked up the first cup. She sniffed it. "Apples!" she said. "I used my nose." Dad laughed. "Good. Smelling uses your nose."

The next cup had crunchy crackers. Chloe took a bite. Crunch, crunch. "I hear them!" she said. "Ears!" Dad clapped. "Yes. But crunchy crackers have a trick." He held her nose and her ears went quiet too. "Stop!" said Chloe. "The crunch went away!" Dad smiled. "Your ears and nose help each other. Now look at the last cup."

Chloe peeked in. She saw red jam. "My eyes saw it first!" she said. Then she touched the cold cup. "And my fingers felt it!" Dad gave her a lick of jam. "Mmm. My tongue," said Chloe. She counted on her fingers. "Nose, ears, eyes, fingers, tongue. Five!"

"Five senses," said Dad. Chloe licked the jam off her thumb. "Can we play again tomorrow?"

Andrew went to the pool by the lake. He wanted to swim like the big kids. But his feet would not come up. He stood on the steps and watched. Then he saw his friend Sam. Sam took a big breath and held it. Sam's legs came up like a boat. Andrew took a big breath too. He held it and held it. His legs popped up to the top. "Look at me!" he said. He kicked his feet in the water. Then he put his feet down and stood. He was tired and a little shy. "Good job," said Sam. "Try again." So Andrew waited a bit. He took another big breath. He held it, and up came his legs again. He kicked all the way to Mom. Mom clapped her hands. "Big breath, then float," said Andrew. After swimming, Andrew was sleepy. He had his nap under a big tree by the lake. The water went lap, lap, lap on the shore. Andrew dreamed of kicking his feet. When he woke up, he said, "Pool again tomorrow, Mom?"

Chloe wanted to make her own breakfast. "I can do it," she said. Daddy gave her warm toast and a little knife.

Chloe pushed the butter hard. The toast slipped off the plate. It landed on the floor. "Oops," said Chloe. Daddy laughed. "Try little taps," he said. Chloe tapped the butter. Tap, tap, tap. The butter spread all over. "Little taps work," said Chloe.

Next came the milk. Chloe held the cup up high. She poured fast. Milk splashed on the wall. "Oh no," said Chloe. She looked out the window. The sky looked stormy, and the milk on the wall looked stormy too. Daddy wiped it with a towel.

Chloe set the cup low on the table. She poured slowly. Not one drop spilled. She drank it all up. "The cup stays still when it sits down," said Chloe. Daddy took a big bite of toast. "Yum," he said. "Best butter in town."

Emilia ran to the clinic door. Today she would get a shot! A long line of kids stood by the desk. Emilia got in the line too. She hopped from foot to foot.

"Will the shot hurt a lot?" she asked her mom. "The nurse will count," Mom said. "Then it is done fast." Emilia waited. Her tummy felt jumpy. Her legs felt weak, like noodles.

At last it was her turn. The nurse smiled. "Look at the wall," she said. "I will count to three. One, two, three!" A tiny pinch came. Then it was over! Emilia looked at her arm. The bandage was already on.

"It is done!" Emilia shouted. "The count made it fast!" She jumped off the bed. Her legs felt strong now. She ran to show Dad the bandade. "Look, Dad! I got a shot, and I did not cry!"

"Wow," said Dad. "Can I see your brave arm?" Emilia held it up high.
